Sameeran My association with Chennai began in 2013 when I first came to the city after being assigned to the Tamil Nadu cadre. What began as a posting gradually became something more personal — the city became home, says Greater Chennai Corporation Commissioner G.S. Sameeran. After spending 10 years across different field postings in the State, returning to Chennai and settling here felt like coming back to a familiar place. Chennai’s greatest strength is, perhaps, its multicultural spirit — a city that has welcomed people from across the country, giving them not only opportunities, but also a sense of belonging and a place to build their lives. What I love most about Chennai is its ability to be modern while firmly holding onto its traditions and values. Above all, the hard work, warmth, and resilience of its people have touched me the most. Chennai has a style and swag of its own — from its distinctive dialect to its unique way of doing things. As the GCC Commissioner, I now have the privilege of contributing to the city I have come to love. The GCC’s focus is on making Chennai more disaster-resilient, pedestrian-friendly, and better connected through multi-modal mobility. We are strengthening its blue-green infrastructure, creating more public spaces, and making the city greener, with a target of planting 12 lakh saplings this year. I feel grateful to be a part of this remarkable city. Chennai is not merely a place where I have lived or worked; it is a city that has, in its own quiet way, become a part of me. title: The Motorcycle You'll Probably Keep Longer Than Your Car - Top Speed
content: Abhik has been an automotive journalist for over 14 years, with expertise in both motorcycle and car road testing, reviewing, as well as writing and executing feature travelogs. He has worked for Indian brands including Evo India Magazine, Auto Today by India Today Group, and anchored video reviews for Powerdrift Studios. He also has keen interests in most forms of motorsports, having competed in a couple of seasons of one-make racing with TVS Racing on two wheels and Volkswagen Motorsport on four. Alongside his motoring pursuits, e-sports and sim racing are current interests, as are cycling and cycling tech. The love for motorcycles, they say, is an everlasting one. One man proved it, as much for himself as he did for the rest of the world. Helge Pedersen, a Norwegian photojournalist from Kristiansand, sold nearly everything he owned, bought one of the first BMW R80 G/S motorcycles to reach Norway, and spent the next decade riding it around the world. Ten years and 250,000 miles later, after becoming the first to cross South America into North America through the roadless Darien Gap, the bike he called Olga was still the same one he'd left home on. If that sounds inspirational, and you want one long-term bike as well, we have a solid recommendation for you. It belongs to an adventure bike lineup with an illustrious history and to a brand that usually makes long-lasting premium machines. BMW back then set the tone for ADVs to follow as the GS cemented its place in history with four Paris-Dakar wins in the early 80s. Of course, back then, options in this new category of bikes weren’t many outside the endurance rallying circuits, and adventure riding itself was a concept reserved for a few like Pedersen. Today, things are very different, and choices are aplenty. S&P Global Mobility (now Mobility Global) puts the average vehicle on American roads today at 12.8 years old, which, surprisingly, is a record high and still climbing. The number blends brand-new leases with tired commuter cars, so it says little about loyalty than it does about people simply holding onto what they already have for longer. A motorcycle that intends to stay in the same garage past that mark, then, needs to be special. One that has almost nothing to prove now because its history is rich enough to have countless examples of it roaming various parts of the planet, some even in areas untouched by other vehicles. The problem with choices is that the modern motorcycle is a tech-laden spaceship on two wheels. Pick a flagship-grade adventure bike, and you’re guaranteed the latest and greatest in electronic tech that’ll help you reach further into the wilderness. The part where the machine is solid enough to get you there and bring you back, now that isn’t something you can simply haggle for in a showroom. That’s built on the kind of legacy that the GS series of motorcycles almost exclusively enjoy. And the R 1300 GS is the latest flag bearer with ample reasons to be your forever bike like its predecessor. The current R 1300 GS starts at $20,395 and replaces the 1250's engine with a completely redesigned 1,300cc ShiftCam BMW boxer, a new two-part frame, and the EVO Telelever front end, an evolution rather than a reinvention of what's kept the platform trustworthy this long. It's a familiar shape too, but with a new face and bodywork, packed with a new engine making 145 hp and 110 lb-ft while running smoother through the rev range than the boxer twins that came before it. BMW is no stranger to premium engineering, and the 1300 GS is simply built to last. One of the ways it does so is also by simplifying its upkeep. For starters, the 1300 GS needs to visit a service center every 6,000 miles for an oil change and every 12,000 for a valve clearance check on the ShiftCam system. The shaft drive removes any need for chain adjustment or maintenance at the service center or by yourself. The horizontally opposed boxer layout also runs with less inherent vibration, so that’s a structural head start in relieving the rider of additional fatigue from vibrations. This, in no measure, is a small feat, as vibrations, especially over distances, are a major contributor to fatigue, and the big GS eliminates it. This combination of low and easy maintenance simply makes owners keep riding it worry-free. It’s also why generations of GS owners have pushed their bikes past six figures on the odometer without a rebuild. To make the initial ownership even simpler, BMW backs the R 1300 GS with a 3-year, 36,000-mile warranty, a stretch long enough that most owners will clear several service intervals before they ever need to use it. While the reliability of the R 1300 GS is unquestionable, the chassis backs up the engine with ample tech of its own. The EVO Telelever front end and EVO Paralever rear, working with a new monocoque frame, give the R 1300 GS a planted, communicative front end that riders trust on loose surfaces without the need for constant electronic intervention to stay upright. Another reason for the big GS to be your do-it-all forever bike is the advanced suite of electronics that provide a layer of tech that’ll keep it future-proof. Four standard ride modes plus an optional Dynamics Package covering Pro-level settings and electronic suspension. This means that the same motorcycle can be dialed in for gravel or the interstate without feeling out of its depth in either environment. The optional Automated Shift Assistant (ASA) adds another way the GS avoids being outgrown, letting a rider swap the clutch lever for fully automatic shifts or flick through gears manually with paddle triggers on the handlebar. This matters most years down the road, when a bad wrist or an aging clutch hand might otherwise be the reason for a rider to give up on riding. There are numerous people who keep cars for a long time, and only a few adventure bikes can make that cut to share the garage space with equally iconic cars. Honda's Africa Twin Adventure Sports ES DCT is built on the same reliability-first premise with comparable pedigree to boot. At $18,599, it undercuts the GS by nearly $1,800, and its 1,084cc parallel twin makes a more modest 101 hp and 82.6 lb-ft. But what’s more enticing for long-term ownership is Honda's own reputation for engines that simply don't quit. It also boasts Showa electronic suspension and a tech suite to cover similar ground as the GS, but the current Africa Twin platform has only been in production since 2016, against the GS boxer's continuous refinement since 1980. Ducati's Multistrada V4 sits closer on price, starting at $19,995, and it out-muscles the GS outright with 170 hp and 91 lb-ft from a 1,158cc V4. The V4 Granturismo engine inside it also breaks with Ducati's own desmodromic tradition specifically to chase long-term reliability, and the payoff is a 37,000-mile valve service interval, roughly triple the GS's. The Multistrada, though much loved for its versatility, has only used its V4 Granturismo engine since 2021. Thus, the GS stands apart with its boxer architecture that has already spent more than four decades proving itself in the hands of owners racking up countless miles on and off the beaten path. It has all the makings of a bike that can even replace everything in your garage, maybe even the car. We want to hear from you. Their clientele and reputation have grown every year — locally and nationwide. The very first boneless ham he and cohort Jamie Steward entered in a national competition in 2022 won the Grand Champion Award at the American Cured Meat Championships. title: FOR SALE: 1957 Porsche 356 A Carrera 1500 GS Coupe by Reutter - Sports Car Digest
content: One of the most desirable and historically significant variants of the early 356 Now offered for sale through RM Sotheby’s Private Sales, this 1957 Porsche 356 A Carrera 1500 GS Coupe by Reutter represents one of the most desirable and historically significant variants of the early 356. Sold new to a U.S. Air Force serviceman stationed in Japan and equipped with sought-after Rudge wheels, the car combines exceptional rarity with an important place in Porsche’s performance-car lineage. The Carrera name was introduced in response to Porsche’s growing success with the 550 Spyder in the demanding Carrera Panamericana. To bring some of the Spyder’s competition-bred character to the road, Porsche adapted a detuned version of Ernst Fuhrmann’s sophisticated 1.5-liter, four-cam, twin-spark racing engine for a limited-production version of the 356 A. Unveiled at the 1955 Frankfurt Motor Show for the 1956 model year, the Carrera established a designation that would ultimately become synonymous with Porsche’s highest-performance road cars. The Fuhrmann-designed engine was available across the 356 A Coupe, Cabriolet, and Speedster ranges. Its advanced construction included roller-bearing crankshaft technology, a dry-sump lubrication system, chrome-plated cylinder bores, and an 8.1:1 compression ratio. Power was delivered through Porsche’s improved Type 644 four-speed transmission, while the dry-sump oil tank was positioned within the left-rear fender well and protected by a mesh screen bearing the car’s chassis number. Twin Autopulse fuel pumps and a pressure-regulating valve completed the specialized fuel system. Porsche also enhanced the Carrera’s chassis to complement its increased performance. title: Which Song From Karol G’s ‘No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto’ Is Becoming the Album’s Viral Breakout Hit? - Billboard
content: This week's Trending Up looks at a gradually building viral hit from Karol's latest, as well as an exploding Cody Johnson deep cut and some tribute streams for the late Hayden Panettiere. Welcome to Billboard Pro’s Trending Up newsletter, where we take a closer look at the songs, artists, curiosities and trends that have caught the music industry’s attention. Some have come out of nowhere, others have taken months to catch on, and all of them could become ubiquitous in the blink of a TikTok clip.  This week: Karol G may be on her way to a slow-building breakout hit from her latest semi-surprise album, while Belly Gang Kushington’s mainstream crossover continues and fans mourn the late Hayden Panettiere. Following the Aug. 7 release of No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, her sixth full-length studio album, Karol G scored her fifth No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Latin Albums chart. The deeply personal and sentimental project sits at the opposite end of the mood and emotional spectrum from her 2025 release, Tropicoqueta. The album’s standout collaborations with Bruno Mars and Drake both entered the charts. “Ahí,” featuring Drake, debuted at No. 1 on the Hot Latin Songs chart, dethroning Bad Bunny’s “DtMF” after a record 72 weeks at the top. “Still,” her collaboration with Bruno Mars, also scored the set’s highest debut on the Billboard Hot 100, entering at No. 41. It’s not the Colombian star’s collaboration with either of those household-name artists, however, that’s really taken off from the album on social media. That would be “BbY WOW,” with Spanish artists Judeline and Risowsky, which has emerged as a fan favorite. The track propelled both Spanish newcomers into the top 10 with their first Billboard-charting entry, opening at No. 5 with 4.5 million U.S. streams. And “BbY WOW” has been rising in streams since its release, totaling over 2.4 million official on-demand U.S. streams over the first three days of this tracking week (Aug. 14-16) — a gain of 28% over the 1.9 million streams the song received its opening weekend. While the album’s moody and sorrowful tone — centered on heartbreak — is evident, “BbY WOW” stands out as one of the most danceable songs on the 14-track project. The song, which describes someone’s surprise at how much they like something, features an interpolation of the Coolie Dance Riddim, which has also been used as the soundtrack for backstage content and in hit songs such as Pitbull’s “Pull Up (The Culo Remix)” and Nina Sky’s “Move Ya Body.” – CATA BALZANO After being named Billboard’s Hip-Hop Up-And-Comer for the Month for March and earning breakthrough hits with “Friend Do” (with YK Niece) and “Tell Me Now” (with Dess Dior), ATL rapper Belly Gang Kushington is eyeing another potential smash. According to Luminate, his 21 Savage-assisted “WTF Goin” has jumped 37% in official on-demand U.S. streams over the past seven weeks. The biggest gains have come over the past two weeks thanks to a pair of viral TikTok trends. On July 31, user @/notkaitlynntttt shared a video of her and her girlfriends twerking in a line, and that clip has since garnered over 1.7 million views and nearly 260,000 likes. In the first week following that video and its subsequent virality (July 31-Aug. 6), “WTF Goin” collected 1.495 million streams, up 25% from the week prior. By Aug. 9, user @/he2hollywooddd shared a “male version” of the trend, trading the twerking for tripping out and hip thrusts. That clip has racked up over 617,000 views and 82,000 likes. During the week of Aug. 7-13, “WTF Goin” streams spiked a whopping 88% to over 2.8 million official on-demand streams. The official “WTF Goin” TikTok sound currently plays in over 653,000 clips. With Belly Gang’s momentum continuing to build and the imminent football season promising a touchdown “celly” dance or two, “WTF Goin” certainly has room to grow as we enter the fall. — KYLE DENIS Hayden Panettiere’s death this Sunday (Aug. 16) shook the entertainment world when it was revealed earlier this week, with an outpouring of grief from fans and peers over the 36-year-old’s far-too-early death. Most of the memories shared were of Panettiere as an actress, for her celebrated roles in sequels to Scream and Bring It On or as cheerleader Claire Bennet at the center of NBC’s late-’00s sci-fi sensation Heroes. But in one of her signature performances — as fictional rising country star Juliette Barnes in the ABC (later CMT) musical drama Nashville — she also did a fair amount of singing. So for many of those mourning the late star, it was a logical time to head to some of that show’s soundtracks of in-universe Barnes smashes like “Love Like Mine” and “Telescope.” Consequently, the collective streams for Nashville Cast (which all the soundtrack songs were collectively credited to) totaled 178,000 official on-demand U.S. streams on the day following her death (Aug. 17) — a gain of 367% from the previous Monday, according to Luminate. And while Panettiere’s recording catalog outside of Nashville was not extensive, she did have a couple songs that appeared in movies that also received significant streaming bumps over the same time period — like “I Fly” from Ice Princess (up over 4,000% to 7,000 streams) — as well as a cover of “Cruella de Vil” from 101 Dalmatians, recorded for 2007’s Disneymania 5 compilation (up nearly 1,900% to over 2,000 streams). – ANDREW UNTERBERGER Earlier this summer (June 26), country star Cody Johnson unleashed his tenth studio album, Banks of the Trinity. The LP’s fourth track, “Take Me Back (Leave Me There),” isn’t an official radio single, but a viral a cappella performance video and romantic TikTok trend have given it a major streaming boost. Over the past five weeks, “Take Me Back” vaulted 150% in streaming activity. Back on June 4, about a month after he first released the song as a promotional pre-release single, Johnson shared an a cappella rehearsal video, which earned over 2.2 million views and 381,000 likes. By July 31, the official Warner Records Nashville TikTok account shared another a cappella clip, with this one being filmed against a gorgeous sunset. That post earned over half a million views, making it the third-most viewed TikTok on the Warner Records Nashville account. The following week (July 31-Aug. 6), “Take Me Back” garnered 2.89 million official on-demand U.S. streams, up 13% from the week prior, according to Luminate. A larger TikTok trend built around romantic couples reflecting on their longevity has also picked up steam over the past two months, with some clips hitting the one-million view mark. Furthermore, about two weeks ago (Aug. 2), Boyz II Men — who joined Johnson for a surprise performance of “On Bended Knee” during his Stagecoach set this spring — shared an a cappella rendition of the sweet ballad to their official TikTok account, collecting 24,000 views. During the week of Aug. 7-13, “Take Me Back” jumped another 24% to over 3.59 million streams. With Banks of Trinity holding strong on the Billboard 200 (it ranks at No. 150 on the Aug. 22-dated chart), CoJo just might have another hit on his hands. – KD A daily briefing on what matters in the music industry A daily briefing on what matters in the music industry Billboard is a part of Penske Media Corporation. © 2026 Billboard Media, LLC. title: Karol G Floods Hot Latin Songs Chart With ‘No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto’ - Billboard
content: Judeline and Rusowsky score a breakthrough with "BbY WOW," the highest charting collab by a Latin act. Sr. Charts & Data Analyst (Latin & Billboard Español) It’s a big week for Karol G on the Billboard charts. Her sixth studio album, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, becomes her fifth No. 1 on Top Latin Albums, while its tracks storm Hot Latin Songs, Hot Latin Pop Songs, Hot Latin Rhythm Songs and Hot Regional Mexican Songs charts (dated Aug. 22). Starting with Hot Latin Songs, Karol pushes Bad Bunny’s “DTMF” down to No. 2. The latter has spent 72 nonconsecutive weeks at No. 1 since its first week on top in January 2025. That 72-week haul stands as the longest command in the history of the nearly 40-year-old tally, which mixes streaming activity, radio airplay and digital sales into its formula. Fueled by streaming activity, Karol G’s “Ahí,” with Drake, bows at No. 1 after registering 5.9 million official on-demand streams in the United States during the tracking week ending Aug. 13, according to Luminate. That sum sends the song to a No. 46 start on the overall Streaming Songs chart and to No. 1 on Latin Streaming Songs. “Ahí” puts Karol G and Drake back on top of Hot Latin Songs — more than two years after their last reigns. Karol’s “Si Antes Te Hubiera Conocido” matched the chart’s longest run of 2024, ruling for 14 weeks (starting July that year). While Drake’s “Gently,” featuring Bad Bunny, held the crown for one week in late 2023. The song makes waves across Billboard’s charts, debuting at No. 44 on the all-genre Billboard Hot 100 and No. 103 on the Billboard Global 200, powered by 11.8 million global streams. It also launches at No. 1 on Hot Latin Rhythm Songs and No. 17 on Latin Rhythm Airplay. Back on Hot Latin Songs, Spanish newcomers Judeline and Rusowsky crash the top 10 with their first Billboard-charting entry, the co-billed “BbY WOW,” with Karol G. It opens at No. 5 with 4.5 million U.S. streams — the highest debut by a Latin act on the current chart. “When Karol first reached out and asked me to write for the album, I was in the middle of my first arena run, so everything already felt a little surreal,” Lara Fernández Castrelo, known as Judeline, tells Billboard. “I ended up cowriting four songs, and as we worked together, I realized Karol and I were going through a very similar place emotionally.” Judeline also has writing credits on three other No Me Arrepiento tracks that landed on the chart: “Matadora” and “Te Llevas To” at Nos. 4 and 6, respectively, while “Final Feliz” debuted at No. 14. “When I wrote ‘Final Feliz,’ I immediately felt like it was a song she had to sing,” Judeline adds. “Then she invited me to be part of ‘BbY WOW’ with Rusowsky, someone I’ve made music with for years, which made the whole experience even more special. title: Longtime G.S. visitor’s book about love of sand castles leads to book in Gulf Shores & Orange Beach - Mullet Wrapper
content:
Crumley asks: “What does the sand teach a man willing to kneel down and listen’’ “What does the sand teach a man willing to kneel down and listen?”
That is the question Charles E. Chumley answers in his book, Every Grain Is Real – What The Sand Teaches.
Morning after morning, whenever he’s in Gulf Shores, Chumley walks down to the beach and builds a sandcastle. He started the practice on vacations about twenty years ago.
After retiring, it became a daily ritual across two beaches, Playa del Carmen and Gulf Shores. What began as something to pass the time quietly became something else entirely.
“What begins as the story of a man who builds extraordinary sandcastles quietly becomes a master class in how to live. Chuck writes about failure, discipline, attention, and generosity with a precision and warmth that I found genuinely transformative. I laughed out loud. I took notes. I aspired to be better,” said Russ Powell, a San Francisco based leadership coach, about the book.
Every Grain Is Real is a memoir in forty-four chapters about daily practice, the people who show up alongside you, and what gets built when no one is watching. Each chapter closes with Bucket Wisdom, a distillation short enough to carry in a pocket.
“For years now, whenever I’m fortunate enough to be on the beach in Gulf Shores, usually in the early morning before it fills up, I build a sandcastle,’’ Chumley said.
“It’s set in part right here on Gulf Shores beaches, and one chapter centers on a local inspiration, Janel Hawkins from Sand Castle University,’’ he added. “Many locals and visitors would recognize her, and her quote is on the back of the book.’’
Hawkins’ quote tells Chumley’s story in a single sentence: “Sand sculptures, just as life, are not made to last forever. That makes them more valuable, not less. Enjoy it while you can and appreciate it when it’s gone,” she said.
Chumley said 100 percent of his author royalties will be donated to Family Promise, a non-profit that works to fight homelessness. The donations will be split between the Baldwin County affiliate and the affiliate near Chumley’s Atlanta home.
The book’s Bucket Wisdom passages include these gems:
• “The best decisions are not made in perfect conditions. They are made by people who are clear enough about what they want that the conditions stop mattering.”
• “Presence is not a technique. It is a decision to be fully in what you are doing.”
• “Different languages, different faiths, different everything. They get along perfectly.”
Chumley spent three decades in corporate America before retiring to find out
what the sand had to say. He lives in Roswell, Georgia with his wife Pam, who he says is quieter and funnier than he is.

In 1990, USA Today formally contacted NASA to clarify rumors about their latest technology, apparently dubbed “sex packets.” Weeks prior, Oakland’s afrosurrealist rap collective Digital Underground (DU) had released their debut album, Sex Packets, themed around a new drug for astronauts that could instantly gratify their sexual desires. As DU’s transgressive lyrics glorified the illicit substance, news of the invention leaked onto the Bay Area’s streets: pamphlets were distributed, and condoms were passed out. NASA was forced to respond to the coital discourse: “NASA has not in the past, nor will they in the future, be working on such a pill … It would be impossible to satisfy the carnal urges of astronauts … To my knowledge, unbridled lust has never interfered with a space mission.” It’s the first and likely last instance of NASA being outmaneuvered by Oakland rappers. (It turned out DU had created the pamphlets and condoms as subversive promotional materials.) The elaborate prank was a piece of artistic genius orchestrated by Gregory Jacobs — the late MC, songwriter, illustrator, pianist and costume-wearing virtuoso known as Shock G. The NASA incident is just one of the many shenanigans detailed in his posthumous memoir, Keep It Beautiful: Inside the Funkyverse of Shock G and Digital Underground, out Aug. 25 — Shock G’s birthday — from Penguin Random House. The book combines handwritten notes, interview transcripts, personal photos and rare sketches compiled by Jacobs’ longtime friend and photographer, Alexis Wolfe Mbassa, who tagged along with Jacobs in order to document his eccentric life for over a decade. The association was intentional; in 2011, Jacobs personally recruited Wolfe Mbassa as a co-author for his autobiography. In 2021, just eight months after submitting the book to literary agents, Jacobs died from a drug overdose in Florida. He was 57. “It was never about money or becoming successful for him; it was about having the freedom to create,” Wolfe Mbassa told KQED. “He put himself in wild situations just to hold on to that freedom.” Wild situations form much of Keep It Beautiful. It details Jacobs’ stints in pimping, homelessness and jail, while containing all of the exuberant, out-of-pocket abundance of a Shock G production. A conversation between Shock G and George Clinton of Parliament Funkadelic? Yup. An African gray parrot named Afro who lives in Shock G’s childhood home and imitates his stepmom, Sonya? That too. One entire chapter is dedicated to his early friendship with a teenage Tupac Shakur, who joined DU as a member before going solo. (Apparently Pac had a “fucked” jump shot in basketball, and no one wanted him on their team). Largely stream-of-consciousness in homage to Jacobs’ creative process, the book is divided into sections based on the regions where he lived. Wolfe Mbassa traveled to each of them to conduct interviews: Topanga Canyon, Hollywood, Los Angeles, Oakland, New York City and Tampa. Jacobs recounts his first job as a 15-year-old, DJing at a local radio station in Tampa. He was fired for disobeying the radio’s directives and opting to spin the full 15-minute version of “(Not Just) Knee Deep” by Funkadelic instead of airing commercials. It isn’t the only example in the book of his natural inclination to rebel. Jacobs extensively details how he evaded authorities, and circumvented court appearances, from age 17 to 22. Even for the most studious hip-hop heads, Keep It Beautiful reveals overlooked wrinkles in Shock’s personality and biography. (Did you know that DU’s original band name was “Spice Regime”?) The book also includes a trove of never-before-seen drawings by Jacobs, showcasing a crude and whimsical style that would come to define his artistry, which sometimes reached ridiculous levels of raunch. (One sketch portrays an anthropomorphic anus forcing an “ASS-PIRIN” pill down its own hole.) But the main thrust of Keep It Beautiful are the granular narratives that Jacobs discloses, like his memories of being jailed in San Diego for six months for grand theft auto, where he used art as a bartering tool. In scattered, disconnected bursts, he and Wolfe Mbassa recount his side quests and failures (such as his brief time as a male “gigolo” in Pennsylvania) revealing the down-bad experiences that molded his worldview before his rap and art careers took off. Glimpses of that fast life can be heard in his lyrics, but the book shows in detail how Shock G actually did get around from coast to coast. At its core, the collage of archival material shows how music and art became Jacobs’ salvation, therapy and refuge. Putting it all together was a joyous challenge for Wolfe Mbassa, personally tasked by Jacobs to retain the book’s silliness and humor. “One of the most difficult parts was trying to figure out how to pull all the pieces together. He always wanted it to be like a scrapbook,” she says. “He wanted it to feel like his personal journals did: stories, mixed with memorabilia and art.” In sitting with Keep It Beautiful, its spiritual thesis is clear: Jacobs’ everlasting search for beauty, creativity and funky originality shone brightest during his darkest hours. It’s about keeping it beautiful, especially when beauty isn’t easily kept. “It was so much fun,” Wolfe Mbassa confirms, “to live in his world.” ‘Keep It Beautiful: Inside the Funkyverse of Shock G and Digital Underground’ will be released on Aug. 25. A free release party with Alexis Wolfe Mbassa and members of Digital Underground takes place Saturday, Aug. 22 at Drake’s Dealership (2325 Broadway, Oakland). Event information here.

Earlier this month, in the midst of touring her Tropicoqueta album, Colombian superstar Karol G unexpectedly released No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, which translates to I Don’t Regret Feeling So Much. The title is an almost perfect thesis for the album: moody, raw, and unfiltered. There are melancholic ballads, including “Después de Ti,” her collaboration with Greg Gonzales of the pop band Cigarettes After Sex, alongside more unruly anthems like “Matadora,” or “Killer.” Fans had reason to suspect something new was coming. Months before the surprise album’s release, Karol began dropping beauty-related hints (unsurprising, as she’s someone known for playing with her hair colors and nails). In January, she posted a carousel on Instagram—including an image of herself wearing rhinestones across her forehead and a baby-blue manicure— captioned: “Unfocused But SparkLYYYY.” It was easy to write it off, as she was in the midst of building the world around her album Tropicoqueta. And in April, at the end of her historic Coachella set, Karol announced she was taking Tropicoqueta on the road. The resulting tour, Viajando Por El Mundo—or Traveling Around the World—seemed poised to continue the same visual language: flowers, fiery colors, and plenty of tropical extravagance. The cover art for “No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto.” But there was another clue for both her new album and “sentimental-blue” era. In one of the promotional videos for the tour, Karol opens a suitcase. Sparkles spill out. She looks at them and says, “No, I’m not packing that one yet.” It was a blink-and-you-miss-it moment, but it now feels like a preview of what was coming. The aesthetic of No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto could hardly be more different from Tropicoqueta. One is fluorescent, maximalist, and celebratory; the other is somber, introspective, and stripped back. On the album cover, Karol appears almost makeup-free and bathed in a cool blue hue—giving the image a nostalgic vibe reminiscent of Britney Spears 2003 album, In The Zone. For Karol, color has always been part of the storytelling, according to Duván Foronda, her makeup artist of nearly a decade. “She is someone who puts color to everything; for her, a song has a color; for her, a feeling has a color.” When they were creating Tropicoqueta, that feeling was happiness. “She said, ‘I want an album that’s really tropical, that feels really happy.’ And to her, the color that expressed that was orange,” Foronda recounts. The beauty followed suit. “That album had a really defined aesthetic,” he says. “In terms of the makeup, we did a lot of red lips, brown lip liner, and orange tinted cheeks.” A close up of Karol G's makeup for her “Viajando Por El Mundo” tour. Now, he’s helping Karol strip things back. Duván, whom Karol affectionately calls “Duvi,” has been part of the process of bringing the singer closer to a more natural version of herself. It’s an interesting evolution for an artist whose beauty identity has always been playful. Before joining Karol’s world, Foronda followed in the footsteps of his mother, Adriana Pérez, a notable Colombian makeup artist. He assisted her on various jobs until eventually building a career of his own, including working with lingerie brand Leonisa—comparable to Victoria’s Secret— which is one of Colombia’s most recognizable brands. There’s something fitting about Karol entrusting this particular beauty transformation to someone who understands the visual language of Colombian beauty from the inside out. For this era, though, the inspiration came from somewhere else entirely: Hawaii. During the trip, Foronda noticed Karol gravitating toward blue. “I noticed she started wearing a lot of blue,” he says. Eventually, she told Foronda why. “She told me, ‘I don't know, this new era, which is more mine, more vulnerable, more personal, feels blue.’” Soon, the color began appearing everywhere. “We would go out with her, and she would wear a blue shirt, sometimes a blue purse, or even a blue phone case,” Foronda recalls. But this isn’t an electric cobalt or the kind of neon blue that might have felt at home in the Tropicoqueta universe. It’s softer, airier. “You’ll notice it's not a vibrant blue; it's like a sky-blue,” he says. “It’s calming.” Karol performing in Los Angeles for her “Viajando Por El Mundo” tour. That sense of calm is starting to make its way onto the stage, too. On her Viajando Por El Mundo tour, which recently stopped in Los Angeles for three sold-out shows with special guests including Becky G and Bruno Mars, the energy of this newer era exists alongside the tropical spectacle that fans have gotten to know. “In the show, we’re still doing the Tropicoqueta [aesthetic], but we’re starting to add some new touches,” Foronda says. “We’re adding Swarovski crystals in her makeup, adding glitter to her makeup, and we’re also doing darker makeup.” It’s the “moodier” makeup, however, that is the biggest departure for the Colombian singer, says Foronda. “In this new era, we’ll see her with makeup that’s darker, riskier,” he explains. The deeper, more undone looks are meant to reveal another side of Karol: the rebellious one. The key to this look is a smudgy eyeliner. “It has to be messy; it can’t be glam or perfect, like a perfect line,” says Foronda. And if that feels like a rejection of the pristine, hyper-polished beauty which has dominated our feeds for years, that’s because it is— at least a little bit. After spending recent years embracing her natural beauty and the soft-focus appeal of “clean girl” makeup, Karol is embracing the mess. More eyeliner. More glitter. More crystals. More drama. The clean girls, it seems, are in fact getting glittery. Foronda’s inspiration board for this new direction is equally sparkly. “I get a lot of inspiration from Zara Larsson’s makeup artist, Sophia [Sinot],” he says. “I love all the glitter she uses, and the little rhinestones she adds to the eyes. I love all the glitter she adds to her body.” His technique is refreshingly low-tech. “I bought an [eyeshadow] palette, and I mix it with body lotion.” The eyeshadow palette is from a New Zealand-based brand, “Question Beauty” while a new MIM body lotion—Foronda’s makeup brand— inspired by a lyric in Karol’s song “Ivonny Bonita” is expected to launch soon and will be available worldwide. Bruno Mars joining Karol on-stage during her "Viajando Por El Mundo" tour in Los Angeles. Of course, underneath all that glitter is skincare. Before a show, skin prep takes priority. Foronda’s secret weapon is a 15-minute Medicube Booster Pro massage that provides temporary rejuvenating effects through LED, microcurrent, sonic vibration, and EMS (electric muscle stimulation), alongside the MIM Hydrating Gel, which contains hyaluronic acid and vitamin B5. Afterward, it’s all about removing what went on. According to Foronda, Karol swears by the MIM Gentle Makeup Remover, particularly when it comes to the layers of mascara required for a stage performance. “For a show, you have to wear a lot of makeup, and that includes heavy mascara,” he says. “And she would always [accidentally] take off all her eyelashes when taking off her makeup.” Now, the remover has become a permanent fixture in Karol’s kit. “She would tell me, ‘There’s no makeup remover like this one.” It’s a small detail, but it captures the beauty philosophy behind this new chapter: the drama can be taken off. The rhinestones can come off. The glitter can be washed away. What remains underneath is the person Karol has been trying to get closer to all along. title: GS Points Leaders Seek Bounce Back This Weekend at VIR - Sportscar365
content: With new co-driver, McCumbee McAleer Racing looking to return to form this weekend at VIR… The IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge GS championship leaders look to rebound from abnormal Road America results for the Virginia Is For Racing Lovers Grand Prix at Virginia International Raceway. Robert Noaker will share the No. 13 McCumbee McAleer Racing Ford Mustang GT4 with new co-driver Finn Wiebelhaus starting at VIR. The No. 13 car has finished in the top 11 in each of the first seven races and built its championship lead from 30 points to 100 entering VIR. Ford scored a pair of podiums at VIR last year in the hands of KohR Motorsports, finishing second and third behind eventual season champions Luca Mars and Jan Heylen in the RS1 Porsche 718 GT4 RS CS. Each of the top five in the championship all finished seventh or worse in the Road America 120. That brought a sixth possible GS title contender into play, in the form of series newcomers YRB Racing and Road America winners Trenton Estep and Allen Patten in their No. 66 Aston Martin Vantage AMR GT4 Evo. The second consecutive first-time GS winners have ascended to sixth and only 190 points out of the lead. A second successive win would propel this team even closer to the front of the pack only a handful of races after debuting at Watkins Glen International following an acquisition of van der Steur Racing. But winning this season has not necessarily been a good thing for GS winners in their next race. In an odd quirk, the results for GS winners in their next race, starting at Sebring, have been 29th, ninth, second, fourth, 21st and 28th, for an average 15th place finish. The gap from first to 15th place in IMSA’s scoring system is, conveniently, 190 points. Mars and Dillon Machavern rebounded with a seventh place in their No. 95 Turner Motorsport BMW M4 GT4 EVO to jump back to second in points. They’re tied with fellow BMW runners Stevan McAleer and Austin Krainz in their No. 27 AutoTechnic Racing BMW and 10 points clear of fourth-placed Michael Cooper and Moisey Uretsky in the No. 44 Ibiza Farm Motorsport McLaren Artura GT4. Winward Racing’s Bryce Ward completes the top five, 160 back, in his No. 57 Mercedes-AMG GT GT4. TCR has, on paper, been a bit more straightforward. The Mason Filippi and Bryson Morris pair secured their sixth podium from seven 2026 starts aboard the No. 33 Bryan Herta Autosport Hyundai Elantra N TCR. They hold a 150-point lead on teammates Preston Brown and Denis Dupont, who share the No. 76 Hyundai. Either or both of these two need a big VIR result to make inroads on the Nos. 33 and 76 cars, which appear set to vie for the title in the last three races. Among the 42 cars split 29 GS and 13 TCR, there are several other changes. CarBahn’s No. 39 BMW is absent this race. CSM now switches to Aston Martin for its two entries, and its second car features Ismaeel Ellahi graduating from IMSA VP Racing SportsCar Challenge alongside Ayrton Houk. Kingpin Racing makes its second start of the season with Patrick Wilmot and Tyler Hoffman. Celso Neto and Eddie Gou, who finished second in TCR at Road America in the No. 55 Gou Racing w/Stallion Audi RS 3 LMS TCR, switch to the No. 77 Stallion Motorsports w/GOU CUPRA Leon VZ TCR this race. There are two one-hour practice sessions Friday, with qualifying Saturday morning and the Saturday race at 2:15 p.m. ET and local time. title: No Regrets, Just No. 1s: Karol G’s ‘No Me Arrepiento De Sentir Tanto’ Debuts Atop Top Latin Albums Chart - Billboard
content: The singer claims her fifth leader on the tally and impacts the Hot Latin Songs chart. Sr. Charts & Data Analyst (Latin & Billboard Español) Karol G’s sixth studio album, No Me Arrepiento De Sentir Tanto, debuts at No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Latin Albums chart (dated Aug. 22), halting Bad Bunny’s reign with Debí Tirar Más Fotos, which has spent a record 77 nonconsecutive weeks atop the list and has been No. 1 since the Jan. 24-dated chart. Karol G’s set also floods Hot Latin Songs with 13 entries, led by “Ahí,” with Drake, which opens at No. 1. No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto was released Aug. 7 via Bichota/Interscope/Capitol, just more than a year after Tropicoqueta led the Top Latin Albums chart for two weeks in July 2025. The new set marks Karol G’s fifth straight debut at the summit among seven career entries — only Unstoppable and Ocean fell short, peaking at No. 2 in 2017 and 2019, respectively. No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto begins with 50,000 equivalent album units earned in the United States in the tracking week of Aug. 7-13, according to Luminate. For its chart debut, the set registered 48,000 from streaming activity, which equals to 49.5 million official on-demand streams. Album sales comprised a little over 1,000 units, with a negligible number of track-equivalent units. With No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, Karol G adds her fifth No. 1 on Top Latin Albums. No other female artist has dominated the overall Latin albums ranking in the past decade like Karol G, who trails only the late Jenni Rivera and Shakira, each with seven No. 1 albums, the most among female artists in the chart’s history, dating to 1993. Meanwhile, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto opens at No. 8 on the all-genre Billboard 200 — Karol G’s fourth top 10 — and breaks through to No. 1 on Top Latin Pop Albums. Plus, the set arrives at No. 7 on Top Streaming Albums. Here’s a rundown of Karol G’s No. 1s on Top Latin Albums: On the tracks front, 13 tracks from the new album join two already charting titles on Hot Latin Songs, which includes streaming data, radio airplay and digital sales into its formula. “Después de Ti,” with duet parter Greg González, and the album’s first charting track, flies 17-10, while fellow advance single “Matadora” slips 4-3. But the biggest winner is “Ahí,” her collab with Drake, which debuts at No. 1 largely by 5.9 million official U.S. clicks. The sum yields a No. 46 start on the overall Streaming Songs chart, and a No. 1 on Latin Streaming Songs. title: Biz Buzz: St. G’s Bodega moving into old hardware store in St. Cloud's East End - St. Cloud Live
content:
ST. CLOUD — A new bodega store, St. G’s Bodega, is scheduled to open in early September on the site of an old hardware store in St. Cloud’s East End. It’ll have staple grocery items with a “New York bodega style,” St. G’s Bodega co-owner Maddie Waseka said. That means sodas, cereals, chips, cigarettes and more will all be for sale. “We wanted to add something that was a little bit higher-end than your standard grocery in looks and offered the everyday staples that people need on that side of town,” Waseka said. The location is 415 E St. Germain St., originally the old Sentinel Hardware building before it was purchased by Marla Waseka, Maddie’s mother, in 2022. The Waseka family, through their real estate restoration company, MoXie Ladies, has for years been purchasing dilapidated real estate on 
    
      St. Cloud’s East End,
    
       or areas centered around East St. Germain Street and the Lincoln Avenue corridors, east of the Mississippi River. The long-closed hardware store now houses 
    
      Respect Fight Club
    
       gym in the basement, breakfast and lunch restaurant 
    
      Kitchenette,
    
       home goods store 
    
      Sage & Salvage,
    
       four apartments and now St. G’s Bodega. Nearby, they also purchased the former Ace Bar building on June 26 with plans to restore it as a bar and restaurant. “It's more of a passion project than anything,” Maddie Waseka said. “We figure if we keep doing our own thing and put cool things in, people will come along behind us and do their own cool things on the East Side.” The St. Cloud Retired and Senior Volunteering Program is receiving a $425,000 continuation grant as part of AmeriCorps’ grant competition for organizations that offer volunteer opportunities for people 55 and older. RSVP
    
       is an AmeriCorps program dedicated to seniors hosted by the City of St. Cloud that serves Benton, Sherburne, Stearns and Wright counties. The program matches seniors with volunteer opportunities that match their interests, skills and schedules. The organization’s 1,200 volunteers have worked alongside more than 160 partner nonprofits, government agencies and healthcare groups. “We’re thrilled to be able to continue serving our communities,” RSVP Director Jennifer Wucherer said in a statement. “We are passionate about working with older adults — not only to help meet community needs, but also to honor and value the experience, knowledge and impact that older adults bring. Service is one of the greatest gifts we can offer and one of the more reliable ways to enrich our own well-being.” Around 130 grants were handed out nationally in 2026, with St. Cloud being one of five organizations in Minnesota to receive the award. St. Cloud Financial Credit Union Executive Vice President Chase Larson, who is also the company’s chief lending officer, is the newest member of the Central Minnesota Habitat for Humanity’s board of directors. The board is responsible for ensuring good financial stewardship and accountability. Chad Bouley, executive director for the local branch, said Larson brings sound business leadership to the organization. “Chase is a proven leader in our community, and his vision, creativity, and passion for serving others will be tremendous assets as we continue to grow our impact. We are excited to have him helping shape the future of our organization and advancing our mission throughout Central Minnesota,” Bouley said in a statement. Central Minnesota Habitat for Humanity and St. Cloud Financial Credit Union have partnered on projects before. Central Minnesota Habitat for Humanity named SCFCU as its 2024 Business Partner of the Year. St. Cloud State University recently won a $135,000 state grant to partner with local machining manufacturer Park Industries to boost workforce development training. That figure rises even higher thanks to an additional $262,000 in matching funds from Park Industries to St. Cloud State’s Professional and Continuing Education (PACE) division. The two-year project will involve customized training, leadership development and digital skills training for 217 employees. The grant supports a "robust" training model designed to address workforce challenges in advanced manufacturing, including skills gaps, leadership readiness, digital transformation and employee retention in a tight labor market. The training initiative is expected to deliver measurable outcomes for both employees and the regional economy. This partnership reflects a shared commitment to building a resilient, inclusive and future-ready workforce across Central Minnesota, according to participants. PACE specializes in building employer partnerships that strengthen regional economies and create long-term talent pipelines. Visit the

title: St. G's Bodega Opens On East St. Germain Street Just In Time For FestFall - WJON
content: ST. CLOUD (WJON News) -- A new place to grab some snacks and other essentials is coming to St. Cloud's East End. Marla Waseka owns the building and will operate the community grocery store with her two daughters. The term Bodega is common in urban places like New York City and basically means a small family-owned store or neighborhood convenience shop. It's kind of a gathering space for the neighborhood.  People are welcome to post neighborhood events that are going on.  It's going to provide some basic grocery items, personal care, and household items. She says they want the store to change and evolve as they get feedback from customers and neighbors. What we are creating here is an urban village, which is a place where everything is provided for the residents in the neighborhood.  There are services for them; there are shops, restaurants, and bars.  So eventually we could become a little self-sufficient neighborhood of our own. St. G's Bodega will have four tables and chairs in the front by the windows for people to sit and gather. Eventually they'll offer some prepacked sandwiches and other grab-and-go foods, lunches, etc. The Old Dutch Maid Bakery awning may also be brought out of storage and repurposed in some way in the bread aisle. Waseka says she plans to keep the vibe of a 1920s-era grocery store feel. The St. Cloud City Council approved their tobacco license on Monday night. Maddie Waseka opened The Kitchentte next door to St. G's Bodega a year ago on Festi-Fall weekend. Earlier this year, Marla Waseka bought the former Ace Bar building with plans to renovate that and reopen it as a bar and restaurant in the next few years. title: State Department Expands Schedule Policy/Career Push as Other Agencies Could Follow - FEDmanager
content: The State Department is reportedly expanding its push to classify more workers into the new Schedule Policy/Career category. According to GovExec, that includes expanding the search to identify more employees in the General Schedule (GS) 13 and GS-14 levels for possible conversion. The move is raising concerns among federal worker groups that other agencies could follow the State Department's approach. This comes after President Trump signed an executive order in June that reclassified approximately 8,000 employees into Schedule P/C, short of the 50,000 or so positions who were projected to possibly move into Schedule P/C. The new category reduces some of the traditional civil service protections available to employees, including protections related to adverse personnel actions. According to one State Department employee who spoke to GovExec, human resources officials at the State Department are “using a short questionnaire to determine if GS-13 and GS-14 level employees are working in policymaking positions that should be reclassified to Schedule P/C.” The questionnaire reportedly includes questions on whether a particular position formulates policy, develops regulations, provides substantive advocacy of foreign policy, represents the department before Congress, as well as other questions. The push to convert more GS-13 and GS-14 employees comes after a senior administration official said that 97 percent of employees converted so far are at GS-15 or higher. The official said a “small number” of GS-13 and GS-14 employees were also converted, but that most of them work at the Office of Management and Budget (OMB). A second staffer told GovExec that while the work is in the early stages, it’s moving “relatively fast.” OPM says the creation of the new category is necessary to ensure that federal employees holding policy making or policy influencing positions “can be held accountable for poor performance or misconduct. “ The creation of Schedule Policy/Career also remains the subject of legal challenges brought by groups including the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE), Democracy Forward, and others.
